personas.why: The flickering knee dot makes a bad count feel like a bug I could actually diagnose. I'd save the diagram; the exam analogy slows me down.
Fourteen versus eleven is a discrepancy I want explained. When the counter does the same reveal again, I assume I've already seen the interesting bit and swipe just before the cause.
I'd watch to see what a bad squat looks like. The skeleton catches my eye, but '17 joints' sounds like the start of a software walkthrough.
A warning before a bad rep sounds useful. Once I see it's an old clip and the next question is how the tracker works, I'm not waiting for the warning.
I can follow the whole mistake: a dip means a rep, the machine hides the knee, the count goes wrong. It feels finished at eleven. A second diagram looks like another lesson.
The knee line peeling off into a wave is the bit I'd send to my project group. I can picture building the counter, and FORM gives me somewhere to start.
Seeing suspect dips grey out is satisfying: I can see why the number changed. I already get the idea of a personal baseline without the exam-paper example.
The corrected count is a result. The dashed judge is a proposal. I'd stay for a second set that tested the rule, not a diagram of what it might decide.
I'd screenshot the solid-versus-dashed diagram. It's a compact way to show a teammate what a prototype does today versus what the creator wants it to do.
I want to know whether the tool would change the decision to keep lifting. By the second title card, I've seen it fix a count, but the decision is still labelled 'next'.
The red strike buys the first three seconds and the hidden-leg zoom earns my attention back. The exam doodle keeps explaining a point the title card already landed.
The opening counter tells a neat little story even on mute. Seventeen seconds later I recognise the same strike-through, not a new twist worth waiting for.
Rejecting an unreliable detection instead of guessing is a design choice I can reuse. I'd comment for the skill to see what the separate coach check actually takes as input.
I'd save the occlusion example: footage, keypoint and signal error are visible together. Agreement on eleven is interesting; it doesn't tell me the form verdict is reliable.

I stay for the replay because a machine blocking the camera is a real filming problem. Depth and steady reps are useful observations, but I can't see the knees clearly enough to send a client that green GOOD SET card.
I don't need to know AI to spot the rail hiding his leg. Once the count is fixed, I'd rather see another lifting clip than read the boxes above his face.
